newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SA WEEK AHEAD - FOCUS ON RAND, WORLD AWAITS FOMC.
newsitem.headline: SA WEEK AHEAD - FOCUS ON RAND, WORLD AWAITS FOMC.

text.p: The focus will remain on South Africa's fragile rand this week in the absence of any significant domestic economic data.

Markets start the week edgy, digesting remarks by Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals on Friday that scrapping exchange controls could take four to five years -- ruling out the possibility of a "big bang" abolition.

President Nelson Mandlea also injected fresh political uncertainty into proceedings with weekend comments that he has not endorsed his deputy Thabo Mbeki as his successor, saying it was a decision for the party to take.

Meanwhile, currency dealers are nervous following news that Finance Minister Trevor Manuel has appointed a committee to investigate the provision of forward cover in the foreign exchange market, in view of heavy losses this year.
Internationally, a meeting of the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) and Japanese September trade and current account data will be the main highlights for financial markets in the coming week.
While Wednesday's FOMC meeting is expected to bring no change in interest rate policy, it will still be a focus.

"The economic slowdown and continued good behaviour of inflation mean people are going to be fairly relaxed (about interest rates)," said Ian Harwood, head of strategy and economics at Kleinwort Benson in London.
He said there would still be some residual anxiety that the Fed may raise rates, but it was most unlikely to happen.

U.S. October producer price and consumer price data, on Wednesday and Thursday respectively, will affect bond market sentiment quite materially if they come in higher than expected, but forecasts were muted, analysts said.
Harwood said Thursday's October retail sales and Friday's industrial production were also likely to show continued easing of economic growth.

In Japan, markets will be looking for comments and indications about dollar/yen after comments from Japanese Ministry of Finance official Eisuke Sakakibara on Thursday that the dollar's recovery was about to end.
"The Japanese current account figures will be influential there," said Paul Donovan, senior economist at UBS in London.
The September trade balance and current account data, to be published Monday, are expected to justify the shift in policy and indicate a stronger yen policy in the future.
"The weak yen policy has been very useful in stimulating the Japanese economy but has outlived its usefulness," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
He said the pace of decline in the trade surplus was slowing and players would scrutinise the data for signs of confidence that trade trends were changing.

Harwood said trade account data would be watched for a strong revival in exports and a deceleration of import growth. "The trade figures might not be as conducive to good relations between the U.S. and Japan as people have been assuming."
